title: BV treatment online: prescriptions, yeast vs BV, and costs - FutureClinic
summary: Bacterial vaginosis treatment online and yeast infection care: compare symptoms, generic drug prices, and message visits with a licensed doctor for $40.
body_markdown:
Treating bacterial vaginosis (BV) or a vaginal yeast infection starts with telling the two apart and choosing the right prescription, such as oral metronidazole, metronidazole gel, clindamycin cream, or a single fluconazole pill, if your doctor decides it's right for you. Getting evaluated in an office often means a long wait: in[AMN Healthcare's 2025 survey](https://ir.amnhealthcare.com/2025-05-27-New-Survey-Shows-Physician-Appointment-Wait-Times-Surge-19-Since-2022,-48-Since-2004) across 15 metro areas, new-patient waits averaged 23.5 days in family medicine and 42 days in obstetrics and gynecology, while a[2015 American Journal of Managed Care study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26295356/) found an average office visit takes 121 minutes.


At[FutureClinic](https://futureclinic.com/) , you message a state-licensed, background-checked, verified physician (MD, DO or MBBS), never a nurse practitioner or physician assistant. No form is approved in bulk: a specific doctor reads your case and sends your plan with a Human Signature, a short video or voice note recorded live for you. We believe AI is a tool for doctors and the doctor is in charge. FutureClinic's AI works behind the scenes like a chief resident, gathering your history, and never gives medical advice by itself, because we believe the technology isn't safe enough yet and only a human expert knows when AI makes a mistake.


## How do bacterial vaginosis and yeast infections differ?


Per the[CDC's 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8344968/) , bacterial vaginosis (BV) replaces normal lactobacilli with anaerobes like *Gardnerella* . The[HHS Office on Women's Health (OWH)](https://www.womenshealth.gov/a-z-topics/bacterial-vaginosis) notes BV is the most common vaginal condition at ages 15 to 44. Most cases have no symptoms, but[ACOG](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/vaginitis) notes BV causes thin white or gray discharge with a strong fishy odor, especially after sex or during a period, while itching is uncommon.


Vaginal yeast infections ( *Candida albicans* ) affect 75% of women at least once, per the CDC.[OWH](https://www.womenshealth.gov/a-z-topics/vaginal-yeast-infections) and ACOG note yeast causes extreme itching, burning, and odorless cottage-cheese discharge. In a[2002 Obstetrics & Gynecology study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11864668/) of 95 women buying over-the-counter yeast medicine, only 33.7% had yeast, 18.9% had BV, and 21.1% had mixed infections. Over-the-counter yeast creams cannot treat BV.


Because the CDC reports history alone is insufficient to diagnose vaginitis accurately, your doctor may order discounted lab tests (such as self- or clinician-collected vaginal NAAT swabs) or advise an exam for first-time symptoms (when ACOG advises seeing an ob-gyn), persistent or recurrent infections, trichomoniasis (70% to 85% asymptomatic; partners need treatment), or CDC-recommended HIV and STI screening for BV.


## What prescriptions treat BV and yeast, and what do generics cost?


If your doctor decides it's right for you, standard BV and yeast drugs are non-controlled ([DailyMed](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/search.cfm?labeltype=all&query=metronidazole) ). On[Cost Plus Drugs](https://api.costplusdrugs.com/pricelist/cpd) as of October 2026 (before $5.25 shipping), CDC first-line BV regimens are:


-


**Oral metronidazole 500 mg** twice daily for 7 days (CDC-recommended; off-label on tablet label): $5.64 for 14 tablets; can cause nausea or metallic taste.


-


**Metronidazole gel 0.75%** daily for 5 days (FDA-approved): $11.89.


-


**Clindamycin cream 2% (Cleocin)** nightly for 7 days (FDA-approved; may weaken latex condoms and diaphragms for 5 days after use). Yeast develops in 6% to 10% on gel and 10.5% on cream.


CDC alternatives include tinidazole ($17.10 to $20.13), clindamycin capsules ($6.56), clindamycin ovules, or single-dose secnidazole ([Solosec](https://www.solosec.com/bacterial-vaginosis/savings-card) ; 53% phase 3 cure versus 19% placebo; from $75 cash or $25 insured via savings card as of October 2026).


For uncomplicated yeast, the CDC's oral option is one **fluconazole 150 mg pill** ($5.24 at Cost Plus as of October 2026). On the[Diflucan label](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/search.cfm?labeltype=all&query=fluconazole) , one tablet matched 7-day topical azoles (55% therapeutic cure; side effects 26% versus 16%). Over-the-counter miconazole 2% ($9.40), clotrimazole 1% ($8.39) and prescription terconazole 0.8% ($19.96) are other options; the CDC says azole treatments clear the yeast in 80% to 90% of women who finish them. In pregnancy, the CDC recommends metronidazole or clindamycin for BV and 7-day topical azoles only for yeast, as oral fluconazole was linked to miscarriage in a[2016 JAMA study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26746458/) (hazard ratio 1.48).


## Why does BV come back, and where do guidelines disagree?


In a[2006 Journal of Infectious Diseases study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16652274/) , BV recurred within 12 months in 58% of women after oral metronidazole. Douching increases relapse and probiotics lack evidence, per the CDC. Messaging the same doctor lets you retest or discuss suppressive twice-weekly metronidazole gel, vaginal boric acid ([unapproved homeopathic on DailyMed](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/search.cfm?labeltype=all&query=boric) ), or weekly fluconazole for recurrent yeast. For a stable medicine, your doctor can prescribe several months at once when safe.


Sources disagree on two points:


-


**Alcohol with metronidazole** : FDA labels (during and 3 days after) and ACOG (December 2025) warn against alcohol; the CDC (2021) says avoiding it is unnecessary.


-


**Treating male partners** : The CDC (2021) and OWH (2022) say male partners don't need routine treatment, and a[2026 meta-analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41780137/) (6 trials) found no overall drop in recurrence. A[March 2025 NEJM trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40043236/) (164 couples) using oral metronidazole 400 mg plus penile 2% clindamycin cream twice daily for 7 days cut 12-week recurrence to 35% versus 63%. ACOG (December 2025) suggests considering combined treatment, while a[2026 AJOG review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41213492/) notes unanswered questions.
